output.title: When a rollback drill earns its keep
output.body:
For a small-business owner, the cost of a rollback drill is usually not a software question. It is the time spent writing down how to undo a workflow if it breaks, and deciding whether that time is worth it.

A good rule is simple: if the workflow handles money movement, customer data, or repeated handoffs, ask whether you could restore it by hand without losing a day. If the answer is no, or even “I’m not sure,” a rollback drill is probably worth the upfront effort.

That does not mean every process needs one. If a workflow is small, low-risk, and easy to rebuild, the drill may cost more than the failure would.

The practical next step is to pick one workflow and write the manual fallback on one page: what gets paused, what gets checked, who approves the restart, and what has to be re-entered if something goes wrong. That is enough to see where the real cost sits.

Rollback drills are unglamorous, but they are only worth the time when the downside is harder to rebuild than the procedure itself.
